My name is Eddie Summers.

Any middle name or initials that you had? Eddie Milton Summers. Do you mind telling us just when you were born and where? What part of town? Born 1903. Right in New Orleans? September 15th, Port Adler, Louisiana. Where is that, up the river? That's up across the river from Baton Rouge. Oh, sure, I remember that. 1903, September 15th. I wonder if you could tell us a little bit about your father. You just mentioned he played with Claiborne Williams. He played with Claiborne Williams. What was his instrument? Bass violin. Bass violin. Bass violin.
I'd say, Mary, I mean, happy birthday for yesterday, September the 15th. September the 15th. Oh, yeah.
Kid Sheik, both of our birthdays, September the 15th.
Yeah, I remember you used to have a party, you and Noon and Sheik. A party. You used to have a party at Bruce's, didn't you?
Bruce's.
Did you have one this year? We didn't have any this year.
Didn't have one this year. Didn't have one this year.
Didn't have one this year. I know that usually the three of you celebrated. Is it all the same birthday, all three of you?
Sheik and I had the same birthday, same day. September the 15th. When was Noon, Brian, it wasn't the same day. It wasn't the same day. Noon was sometime and sometime, but it wasn't the 15th.

They were all pretty close in there though. It was pretty close to that. Nice parties you used to have at Bruce's. They used to have nice parties. Yeah, they were really good. You were saying, pardon me for anything you were saying about your father.

I never even thought about it when you said the 15th was yesterday. Can you tell us some more about your father? About how old was he and when did he die? Is he still living? He died in 1956. He was 80 years old. 80 years. 80 years old. 80 years old when he died. Did he ever talk about the music? Did he come from up in that part of the area? He come from up there. He come from Moreau, Louisiana. Did he ever play down here that you know? He played with Claiborne Williams. He used to play all around. He used to go all around. He played with Claiborne Williams about the year of 1916 and 17. Did he ever tell you anything about the music when he was a boy up in that part of the country? What kind of dance bands they had I wondered?
He didn't ever tell me anything about the dance bands he had. I remember a couple of you had dance bands.
You heard some when you were a boy too. Did you ever hear the Claiborne Williams? No doubt you did. Oh yeah, sure.
I heard them. Lots of times.
That's before my time. Some of the members are still playing I think up there. Some of the members.
But all those members is dead out now. I don't play with my daddy.
What was your father's name then?
L.M. Summers. Leon Summers.
Leon Summers. Leon Summers.
Yes.
Had he played anything except the string bass? That's all he played, the string bass. Do you remember, were there any brass bands up there that had parades like they do here?
No, they didn't have no brass band up there that they have, yeah.

Your father never mentioned any either that you know of in his time that they had them? Never had them ever mentioned it. Yeah. Because I wondered if they had them out in the country and up in the other towns like Baton Rouge ever. Well sometimes they used to have the farming parade and different parades like that. Did he ever have bands come up there from New Orleans? I know sometimes they go up even now, the Eureka went up a couple years ago. Well we used to go up there, in my time we used to go up to New Roe to play music, play excursions.
Yeah. I used to play up there with Kid René. Oh yeah. You know him?
I knew him before he died. I didn't hear him at about one time is all I ever got to hear him. Kid René, I used to go up there and play with him, Kid René.
Yeah. And Chic was the first one I played with in 1925. 25.

Well tell us about when you first took up music, about how old were you? You took up the bass you just told us you took the... No, no, I took up the bass. I used to practice on the bass when I was a little fella.

About 14, 15 years old. Used your father's bass then? Used my father's bass. Did you have any lessons? Did he help you with it and teach you? He used to teach me but I never played any by bass. Yeah. I was just practicing around the house. Yeah.
You didn't take any other instrument, ever played guitar or anything else? I never played anything else. The trombone. And when did you take up the trombone? 1925. 1925. 1925.
I went on a Vic Gaspar. Oh yeah. You studied with him?

With him. You know I never got to meet him. I was always going to even the day or the week that he died. I had written down on a piece of paper. I was going to go by and try to see him. And I heard suddenly he died. I knew he'd been sick. One of the best. Him and Sonny. Can you tell us more about Vic? What kind of lessons he gave you? I mean what kind of a book he taught and everything that you can remember about him? He taught the white excelsior. The white excelsior? The excelsior book. I have an old mandolin book I believe and I've seen a drum book or something about that same series. Never saw the trombone. Never saw the trombone. It started right at the beginning, did it?
With Vic Gaspar. Mm-hmm. And Sonny Henry gave me a few lessons too. You did hear? Sonny Henry. Yeah. And Yank Johnson. Who was that? I've heard of him.
I never got to hear him. And Buddy Johnson.
And Harrison Bone. You know him? Yes, I knew him.
He died not so long ago. A couple months ago. A couple months ago. A couple months ago. Harrison Bone.
I played actually with the Eureka band, you know? Yes. And Sonny's plays. Sometime Albert plays.

I wonder if you could tell us a little bit more. I'm interested in Vic Gaspar especially since I never got to talk to him or even meet him. Did you hear him with any dance bands much in those days? Oh yeah, there was lots of dance bands. Was he still playing then when you came to town? Oh sure. He's playing. He played at the Lyric Theater. I was in town since 1910. Oh I didn't know. I thought maybe you didn't get here until 1925 or something. No, no, no. Oh you came down early then. Oh I didn't know. Vic Gaspar used to play at the Lyric Theater with John Robichaud.
Yeah, I've heard of that band. John Robichaud. He used to play at the Lyric Theater. He's a good trombone player.

What style did he have? Did he have a big tone? Did he do much sliding? Or was it a rough style or smooth or how? Smooth. He's smooth. Smooth. He used to tell me all the time one good note is better than a thousand bad notes.
Yeah. He's a smooth trombone player.
Good. Did he always play a slide when you knew him or did he ever play the vowel trombone? He played the vowel trombone.

He played the baritone. He played the bass. The bass horn. The big tuba. The big tuba, yeah. He played all that. He didn't play the slide trombone? He played the slide trombone too. Oh he played the slide and the bass horn. Oh he played the slide then? Yes I know he played that. Slide, vowel, and baritone and bass horn. Oh he played the bass horn. He played the bass horn.
When you first got here say 1910 do you remember the first time you heard him was he using the slide then?
He was using the slide up until he died. He went on to the slide. He stuck to the slide.
I wondered if you took up the slide while you were still in town do you know about when he might have taken up the slide trombone or did he play it every time?

He was the oldest trombone player when he started teaching me in town. He was 22 years old playing trombone 22 years when he would take me up. He was the oldest trombone player in town. That was in 1925 then? That was in 1925 he was 22 years old on the trombone.
So he'd been playing since about 1903 then? 1903 or something like that.
1903 something like that. Before we were born. Yeah. Well I was born in 1903. Oh you were born in 1903 then?
I was born in 1905. 1905. Yeah. They look older than you.
Don't go by the looks there though. The Sheik might look older than me too. Yeah I believe he does a little. Sheik born in 1980. Yeah he does look a little older. That's right.
That was 1980. I remember you were saying that you did hear the Claiborne Williams band.
Well I heard the Claiborne Williams band.
What kind of a band was that Eddie?
One of the greatest bands south. Was it a dance band or?
No. Regular orchestra.
Orchestra. They could play all kinds of music. All kinds of music. All kinds of music. He wasn't a fake band. He was a first class band. Used music most of the time.
Music most of the time. He was one of the best bands south. About how big was it? How many?

Well he had about 14 pieces in his band in those days. Pretty big band and used violins. Used violins. He played violin himself. Used violins. He used violins. Trumpet, sax, trombone, bass, piano, drums, all that.

I remember they talk about, was it a Williams that played trumpet? Trumpet, that's his son. That was his son. Was that John? George. George. George Williams. George Williams. George Williams. George Williams.
He played trumpet.
And he had a daughter played piano named Mary, Mary Williams. Oh. But that's after his time. That wasn't in his time. That's his children.

There was one famous trombonist by the name of Williams. I never could find out if he's related. One of the brothers of Claiborne or son too. Is it Williamton? I can't think of his first name now. I know Roy Palmer told me about him, that he was inspired by him. And he traveled with Handy for a while. Johnny Handy? No, no. With W.C. Handy, the St. Louis Blues composer. Oh, St. Louis Blues, I see. He went up to Memphis. I'm not sure he was one of that family, but I always wondered. Well, I wouldn't know him. You didn't remember Williams that played trombone?
I remember Williams played trombone. Oh, but Sam Williams, you know him? No. Sam Williams, he played trombone, but he used to be with Johnny Handy. Yeah, no other. And Kit Howard. Yeah. Clayton.
Did you know any of the members of the Claiborne Williams band by name at all? Do you remember any of the names that were in that band?
You mentioned some of them like the Mary Williams and the trumpet. Any others? Well, see the Mary Williams, they didn't play in that band.

That was the later group. That was the later group. It was Claiborne Williams and LeBlanc, Morris LeBlanc. He used to play. Them was older men. Yeah. Those men around. If they was living, they'd be about 90 years old. Yes. What did he play, LeBlanc? LeBlanc, he played saxophone. Do you remember any other names in the group? Morris LeBlanc. Morris LeBlanc. Yeah. And my daddy named L.M. Summers, or Leon Summers. Claiborne Williams. I see where else they're. I just remember some of those fellas named me. They've been good a while.
Did they use drums in the band? He used drums in his band. I remember the drummer. I guess.

Them was older fellas. Yeah. All the way older, much older than you. Much older than me when they were playing. My dad was playing them from 1917. He quit playing with them in 1918. In 1918. Did your father ever stay where he learned music?
Or where he took up bass?

He took up bass in West Baton Rouge Padres, right? In Port Island, Louisiana. He was raised right in that section? He come there 18 years old. He comes from Monroe, Louisiana. Oh yes. And over upstate. Upstate. That's across from Natchez. Remember up around Natchez, Mississippi? Yeah. He come there when he was 18 years old. Yeah.
Did he ever have lessons on the bass? Or did he pick it up himself, did he say?
Well I don't know how he picked it up. He was way back, was he? I don't know how he picked it up, you know. That was way back.
But he must have been a reading musician.
He's a good musician. He's a good musician. He's a good musician. He's a reading musician. He's a good one. He had to read to play at Claiborne Williams. Yeah, sure.
You say your family moved here in 1910. He would be still playing with Claiborne Williams. He was playing with Claiborne Williams.

In 1910, he was playing with Claiborne Williams then, you know. He was still playing with Claiborne Williams then. He used to go up there in Donaldsonville and travel around with him. Oh, I see. Yeah.
Well, Claiborne Williams' band would be playing all over Louisiana? All over.

All over Louisiana. He lived in Donaldsonville though. Oh, I see. Yeah. My daddy used to go up there and meet him and go different places. They had a good band. They must have been very good. They all around.

They were one of the best bands in the South. They must have been very good bands. How come you took up trombone? How did you happen to pick that? Well, I saw it and I saw one in the showcase and bought it.
I liked it and went to Mr. Vic and gave me a few lessons. I used to be with Sonny. Sonny Henry though, my little boy. Yeah. My little fellow, Sonny Henry.

He'd take me over a while and I went back to Mr. Vic. We had a couple of good interviews with Sonny Henry before he died last year. Yes. I'm still wondering if there's anything else you can tell us about Vic Gaspar. How much did he charge for lessons about? Well, lessons, well he used to only charge 50 cents a lesson. 50 cents a lesson. In them days, you know. Of course, in those days it was a good deal of money too. Good deal of money. Oh, I mean. That's the 25th. That's a good deal of money, right. Right. How long did the lesson last? What did they have you play? Scales and a hook or other things? Scales.

Different thing. Scales, run scales. Put you on one note. Keep you on that one note. A lesson, the whole lesson, you know. Really? Until you get the right tone in that note. He said one good note is better than a thousand bad notes. Yes. That's right. Yeah. Have a fella playing the trombone and make a whole lot of bad notes, blue notes, that's no good. If you make a few notes and they be perfect, that's better.
You know what kind of an instrument he used or he liked? Well, he liked it, he used to use a Holton. Holton, uh-huh.
But I used a CG coin. They're both good makes. He used a Holton, that is his instrument, a Holton.
Did he have you working on long notes, like you said when you worked on that one note?
Yeah, he worked on long, whole notes and all, you know. Half notes, quarter notes. Yeah. He used to make him make triple notes and anything, you know.
Put you on, but just put you on one, you know. Yeah. Did he have anything special about the breathing or anything that he taught you? He taught you how to grip a horn, how to not puff up, you know.

Mm-hmm. The Lord said when you puff up, you can't make the right note. If you want to drop from high to low, you can't drop down there with your mouth puffed up. You got to hold your mouth like you're sucking peas out of a jug or something, you know. Like that. All right, yeah. Then you drop from high down, you know, or go from low up. But if you got your mouth puffed up like that, you can't do that.
He must have been a good teacher.

He's a good teacher. You can't do that if you got your mouth all full of wind, you know. Yeah, that's right. Then you want to go high, you can't do that. I know Bunk Johnson, you know the trumpet player?

Bunk Johnson, yes. A couple of his few died just a few years ago. And I know in New York, he always used to tell Jim Robbins, he said, you ought to go back to New Orleans and take some lessons from Vic Gaspar. Vic was still living, man. I used to tell him. He thought that Vic was about the best one and the best teacher too.

Vic and Sonny were the two best we had you. Teachers and blowing, playing too, you know. Two best we had you for teaching, you know. And playing, but Vic was better than Sonny in the orchestra, you know. Playing in the orchestra. But him and Sonny were tough out there on the screen there. Them two used to play together. Which bands did they play in? They played the Excelsior. They played with the Tuxedo. And they had a band called the Armourish Band too, a long time ago. What's the name of that band? Armourish Band.

Yeah, but if he gets you in his house, then taking lessons, then he'd get strict. Yeah.
Did he give you a lesson to do at home from the method book?
He gave me a lesson to do at home too, you know. And he told me not to take nothing by his head. That's what he gave me, you know.
Then when you went back to him, you had to play that lesson?
I had to play that lesson. I had to play it for him.
To see what I had to study. I had to play it for him. How much did he run you to practice? Did he tell you how much to practice a day or anything? Well, he told me to practice as much as I wanted to.

Yeah. And if you play it like you think it ought to go, he stopped you and said, don't go like that. He said, you're playing by head. He said, play it like I put it there. Yeah.

Then you have to change it, write it down. If he make the, if he flattened the B, if you figure it should be made natural, well you say, well I figure that should be made natural. You see, with the catcher, the tricker, you know. You understand? He know it is wrong, but he wants to see that you know it is wrong. Yeah. You see, if you go ahead and play it like the song written, well he figure you're playing by head. Yeah. And play it like he got it written and he know you're reading. Yeah. You understand that? I was trying to find out that you're reading it or you're playing by head. You understand it, Marshall? Yeah. That's what he want to get to. See what you're reading. He said, see if I know how a Tramon part go, I go ahead and play it like I know how it go. Well he don't have it written like that. He has it written different. He has it written with some false notes in there, you know.
Yeah.
Well you play it with them false notes. Then he say, you alright, you alright. Fix it like it belongs to me. But first you play it the way he wrote it. Play it the way he wrote it, false, you know.
Yeah.
You understand what I mean?
Yeah, that's right, sure.

See he wrote it false and he wants you to play it like he wrote it. He don't want you to play it like a goer, see in head, you can have things in head. Sure. And you can play it in head. Like up a garden in the funeral march, you know. Yeah. You can play it out and play it by head too, you know. But he wants you to play it like he had it written.

He wants you to play it like he had it written. That reminds me of Bunk again, who used to use the Arbonne, the Cornet book. It's the famous great big method for Cornet. And he said the reason he used that, it had so many exercises and things in there. It didn't have much of a tune to it, but you couldn't fake them. You had to stick to that. Couldn't just start playing and guess at it. Couldn't guess at it. Play what you see on the book. Yeah, you had to see exactly what's on there to get it. Uh huh. Play what you see on the book. Oh, you stuck to that white book then, the Excelsior. White Excelsior book, yeah.
I stuck to that.

Any other books that you got later, nothing else later, or any other solos? Did it give you anything else besides that? He used to write me solos. Write them out on paper. Write them out on paper, yeah. Yeah.

Solos for me to play. Yep. And when he see me the next time, he want me to play that, you know. And he want me to play it like he wrote it. Like he written it, you know. He want me to play it like he wrote it. He want me to play it like he wrote it. I want him to play it by head, you know, like I think it ought to go. He want me to play it like he wrote it. Oh, that's your lesson.
Did he ever play with you or play any other? He played with me too, you know.

On trombone? On trombone, yeah. Would he make up a second part or a duets? He could make up a second part. And see on the method that I had, he had trumpet part and trombone part. He had the treble clef and the bass clef. And he could read all of them. He could read the treble and the bass. And see, he'd get on the treble and give me the bass, you know. And he'd go ahead and play along with me, you know.
And he'd been playing in the treble clef?

He'd been playing the treble clef. He could read both of them. He could read all of them clips. Did he just have you to learn the bass clef? Is the only one you learned? He had me learn the bass clef. That's all I, I like the bass clef. But I know when a fella playing the treble clef right. Yeah, I'm sure. In fact, I know when he playing the treble clef right. I can play a little of the treble clef, but I'm more a bass clef man.
Did Mr. Gaspar have a piano there by any chance? Did he ever play on the piano? He played on the piano too. He could play a little bit too, you know. Chords.
Yeah, chords. Chords and the range, I guess.
Arrange, yes.

He was a great trombone player. Baritone, bass violin, bass horn. He played all that. Well, his brother was there. His brother played bass too, didn't he? Oh, yeah. Octave or something. Octave or something. Octave. They called him oak, I guess. Octave, yeah. Octave, yeah.
Octave?
Octave. Oh, Gaspar. Octave, yeah. Octave, yeah.
Octave, yeah. Octave, yeah.

Octave. Octave. Octave, Gaspar.
I haven't heard that.
That's what they called him in Creole, you know.
Yeah.

A lot of those people, they only talked French, you know, and they didn't like to talk English. He could talk plenty English. He could speak good English.
Good English. He's a man about, well, he oughta been about 80 or something too now. I guess he would, oh yeah. About 86, you know.
Yeah, he would.
Way old guy.

He died a little after my dad. September, early in September. I think it was. A little after my daddy died. Your daddy's not been there no more.
It'd be three years. About four years this year. Oh.

You were just a boy. Oh yeah, when we moved here, I was coming up with him.

Yeah. I got some pictures that I had from the Navy there. While I think of it, did you have anybody else in the family that played any uncles or anyone that played music? No, I had an uncle. No, I had an uncle. He used to fool around with a trumpet little bit.
He never had to play to nobody.

He had one at his house playing to fool around with it. Any brothers or sisters in your family that played music? No, no. I'm the only brother. The only one. Is there anything else about lessons with anyone else? Did you take regular lessons with Sonny Henry too? Or did he just help you sometimes?

He helped me. We used to be together sometimes. We used to be drinking a little bit sometimes. He'd take me on by his house and go practice. And then you went back to Vic after that, did you? I was going to Vic all the time. Sometime he'd catch me up here. And him and Vic used to play together in the same band. About how long did you take lessons from Vic Goss?
Vic Goss about two years. You mentioned some other trombonists that you liked or that helped you?
Some other trombone players that I liked that helped me was Harrison Bradley.
Oh yes, Harrison Bradley. That was my friend.
That was another one of my friends. Yes. Harrison Bradley. And William Youngs. No, Albert Youngs.
You know him? No, I never knew him.
Albert Youngs. He went to base there. He had a brother named William Young called Sport. Oh sure, sure. Oh yeah.
What did you know his brother?
Austin. Austin Young. Albert. Called him Albert Youngs. Boots.
One was called Sport and what was the other one called? They had a...

Let's call him Boots. Boots, yeah. That's Albert Young. That's Boots. He's called him Boots for nickname. Yeah. That's like Jim Crow. Yeah. Jam Robinson. I made some records with him playing the string bass with Wooden Joe Nicholas. Boots. Boots, yeah. He's a good trombone player too. Yeah, that's all right. I remember he didn't. He lost his teeth. He wasn't playing anymore. I forget the teeth. He wasn't playing anymore but he played a while after he lost his teeth. Son Henry said he don't understand that fella. Didn't have no teeth and could make any high notes he wanted. He still played. Could still make high notes the fella couldn't make with his teeth.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Thank you.
Yes, he made some records with Bunk one time too on bass in 1942. In 42, yes. The first records that Bunk ever made, he played bass on those and then I had him to read.

segments.title: Opening and Eddie Summers' birth in 1903
segments.summary: Interviewer states date and place; Summers gives his full name and his September 15, 1903 birth near Baton Rouge.

segments.title: Shared birthday with Kid Sheik and Noon
segments.summary: Summers shares a September 15 birthday with Kid Sheik; the trio used to hold parties at Bruce's.

segments.title: His father Leon Summers, bassist with Claiborne Williams
segments.summary: His father L.M. Leon Summers, from Louisiana, played string bass with Claiborne Williams around 1916-17 and died in 1956 aged 80.

segments.title: Country parades and playing excursions upriver with Kid Rene
segments.summary: Farm parades up the river; New Orleans bands came for excursions, and Summers played there with Kid Rene and Chic in 1925.

segments.title: Teaching himself on his father's bass at 14 or 15
segments.summary: He practiced around the house on his father's bass, with some help from his father.

segments.title: Taking up trombone in 1925 and his teachers
segments.summary: He took up trombone in 1925 and studied with Vic Gaspard, Sonny Henry and others, naming Harrison Bradley and more.

segments.title: Vic Gaspard's playing at the Lyric Theater, his tone and instruments
segments.summary: Gaspard played Lyric Theater with John Robichaud, had a smooth tone, played slide trombone, baritone and bass horn, and was the oldest trombonist in town.

segments.title: The Claiborne Williams band: size, style and family
segments.summary: Claiborne Williams led one of the best bands in the South, a reading orchestra of about 14 with violins; his son George played trumpet and daughter Mary piano.

segments.title: Band members and Leon Summers' years with Williams
segments.summary: Names members such as Morris LeBlanc, notes his father played with Williams in 1917-18 and traveled from Donaldsonville around Louisiana.

segments.title: How he chose trombone; Gaspard's lessons, long tones and embouchure
segments.summary: He bought a trombone from a showcase; Gaspard charged 50 cents a lesson, drilled single long notes, taught embouchure.

segments.title: Gaspard and Sonny Henry as the best teachers; Bunk's advice
segments.summary: Bunk Johnson urged Jim Robinson to study with Gaspard; Gaspard and Henry played in the Excelsior, Tuxedo and Armourish bands.

segments.title: Gaspard's reading, appearance and Allen Street property
segments.summary: Gaspard was a first-class reader, tall and light-complexioned, and owned property along Allen Street.

segments.title: Picou, Big Eye Louis Nelson and the Lyric band
segments.summary: Picou played with Gaspard at the Lyric; Louis Nelson succeeded him and always carried his clarinet.

segments.title: Gaspard on holding the horn and wrist vibrato
segments.summary: Gaspard taught holding the trombone level, not puffing the cheeks, and using the wrist for vibrato.

segments.title: Jack Teagarden also took lessons from Gaspard
segments.summary: Summers recalls Teagarden studying with Gaspard, and meeting him again in Los Angeles.

segments.title: Gaspard's homework lessons and practice advice
segments.summary: Gaspard gave lessons to prepare at home, played back at the next lesson, with freedom on practice time.

segments.title: Trick wrong notes to test reading, and the Arban book
segments.summary: Gaspard planted wrong notes to see if he read or played by head; Interviewer compares Bunk's Arban book; Gaspard wrote solos.

segments.title: Playing duets, bass clef and Gaspard on piano
segments.summary: Gaspard played second parts in treble clef while Summers learned bass clef; he also played piano chords.

segments.title: Gaspard's multi-instrument skill, brother Octave and Creole speech
segments.summary: Gaspard played several horns; his brother Octave played bass; he spoke English with a Creole accent.

segments.title: Gaspard's age and death after Summers' father
segments.summary: Gaspard died at about 86 shortly after Summers' father; the family had moved to New Orleans in 1910.

segments.title: Other family musicians and Sonny Henry's help
segments.summary: No family musicians besides an uncle with trumpet; Sonny Henry helped informally, and he studied about two years with Gaspard.

segments.title: Other trombonists: Harrison Bradley and the Young brothers
segments.summary: Summers names Bradley and Albert 'Boots' Young; Boots played with Bunk and Wooden Joe, and made high notes without teeth.
